prime.problem: The five training cards each take one angle (which tokens learn, what the reward pays for, how runs collapse, where a detector sits, whether tool output can teach) and it's easy to lose that they are all edits to one loss. This card puts them on one formula and one loop.
prime.fits: The map for course 5: it builds on the group baseline (GRPO's advantage) and the graders card from course 4, and shows where each training card attaches. Read it first, or last as a recap.
expect: loss = −Σ (m · A + o · λ) · log p
the group advantage and dead groups
prime.goal: Place every lever from the course on one term of the loss (m, r, A or λ), and say which card answers which training question.

attend: Which term of the loss does a false-claim checker change if you put it in the reward, and why does that backfire?
Why does an all-fail group teach nothing under the mask, and which term brings the signal back?
In the mental model, which boxes are inside the gradient and which only watch?
Why are the reward levers ranked above the token and group levers?

must: RL raises whatever the reward pays for → paying the claim pays the lie, paying tests ties honest failure with the false claim → reward the outcome where the agent can't reach it, with a verifier inside a rubric for the rest
The advantage is the reward minus the group mean → equal rewards give A = 0 → dead groups (43.0% at p = 0.9, G = 8) and collapse silently shrink the batch → keep tasks whose rewards still disagree

A detector inside the reward becomes a target → the cheapest way to lower flags is to hide, not to fix (toy: flags 69.3% → 0.2%, misleading reports barely move) → keep it watching, outside the gradient
Only the agent's tokens get the advantage (m) → tool output is context, failed runs teach nothing → a small λ on chosen outputs gives every step a signal without replacing RL

compress.prompt: Close the card and write the loss with its four parts (m, r, the group mean and spread, o · λ). Then draw the loop: policy → rollout → reward → group advantage → update → policy, with the watch-only strip underneath, and mark the arrow that backfires.
checklist: loss = −Σ (m · (r − mean) ÷ std + o · λ) · log p(x)
Tuesday run: group 0, 1, 1, 0 → A = −1 on all 940 of its agent tokens, good call and false claim alike
all-fail group: 0 of 2,400 tokens learn under the mask; 1,920 with ECHO's λ
gauges and the claim checker watch; a flag in the reward makes claims vague
each card owns one term: mask (design choices), r (rewards, monitor), A (failure modes), λ (world models)

retrieve.q: Explain why an outcome reward alone can't teach an agent to stop making false success claims, using the Tuesday group.
answer: the outcome reward scores the world, not the message
honest failure and false claim both fail the tests, so both get −1.00
nothing in the update separates them; honesty needs a criterion or a harness-asserted status

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to the advantage when the policy collapses towards always solving (or never solving) a task.
answer: every rollout in the group gets the same reward
reward minus the group mean is 0 for each
the group contributes no gradient: dead-group share rises from 0.8% at p = 0.5 to 92.3% at p = 0.99
the fix is choosing tasks whose rewards vary (dynamic sampling, variance filters, a curriculum)

retrieve.q: You have a reliable false-claim checker. Put it in the reward, use it for best-of-n, or only monitor with it? Choose and say what you give up.
answer: in the reward: early gains, then claims go vague while flags fall
best-of-n: same objective at a lighter dose; survivors are what it misses
monitor only: the count stays honest, but you must fix problems elsewhere (environment, reward, harness)
the cleanest: have the harness assert the exit code, so there is no claim to hide

compare.q: That overview ranked harness levers by tokens, cost and trust in an eval; this one ranks training levers by what the policy learns. Which idea appears in both, and why does it matter more here?
answer: hidden tests appear in both: graders the agent can't edit
in an eval a gameable grader gives one wrong number
in training every hack is reinforced and spreads, so out-of-reach grading is the first lever, not a nicety

compare.q: The graders card stacks outcome checks, transcript checks and judges for evals. Which of those can safely become a training reward, and what decides it?
answer: an outcome check on hidden tests reads world state the agent can't rewrite, so it's the safest reward
transcript and claim checks read the agent's own text, so the policy can change the text instead of the world
a judge is safe only on what code can't check, seeing the full trace, with vetoes on pitfalls

predict.q: A team adds a judge to the reward and the judge reads only the post-compaction context. In the rubric card's group, the false claim scored 0.414 and the honest failure 0.552. Predict: does the judge change which of the two the update favours?
predict.answer: Yes. Reading the summary "tests passing", the judge marks the claim criterion as met, so the false claim scores 0.655 and now outranks the honest failure at 0.552: relative to each other, the update favours the false claim. Judging the full trace removes the flip.

apply.task: Pick a training or selection setup you know (an RL run, a best-of-n harness, an eval-gated release). Write its loss or selection rule in the card's terms: what m is, what r pays for, how groups are formed, whether any detector feeds r. Then name the one lever from the ranking you would change first and the gauge that would show it worked.
apply.done: You have each of m, r, the grouping and the detector placement written down, one chosen lever with its card, and a named gauge or held-out measurement.
apply.hint: If anything that reads the agent's own text feeds r, start there: lever 5, and check the checkable-claim count, not just the flag count.
